claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating is an FCC single-crystal solid solution without grain boundaries or precipitates.
At 300 K and 600 K, low stacking-fault energy in FeNiCrCoCu promotes partial dislocations and deformation twins.
Partial dislocations and deformation twins act as barriers to dislocation motion, thereby maintaining high hardness and low friction.
In analogous CoCrFeMnNi, stacking-fault energy increases with temperature and suppresses stacking faults and nanotwins.
At 900 K and 1200 K, increased stacking-fault energy in FeNiCrCoCu suppresses deformation twinning and partial-dislocation formation.
Suppression of twinning and partial dislocations causes a transition to full-dislocation glide at high temperature.
Severe lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion in multicomponent FCC HEAs.
Sluggish diffusion makes full-dislocation glide increasingly unstable at high temperature.
Above 900 K, thermal energy facilitates stacking-fault annihilation and rapid breakdown of short-range order.
Stacking-fault annihilation and short-range-order breakdown produce localized incipient amorphization in the indentation zone.
The amorphous layer has lower shear strength and greater adhesion to the indenter than the crystalline coating.
Lower shear strength and increased adhesion in the amorphous layer cause the friction coefficient to spike and wear resistance to collapse.
At 300 K and 600 K, the friction coefficient remains below 0.2 and hardness remains high.
At 900 K, the friction coefficient exceeds 0.4 and hardness decreases by more than 30%.
At 1200 K, the coating exhibits near-liquid-like flow, a friction coefficient above 0.6, and catastrophic wear.
Above 900 K, HCP-like atom counts exhibit a transient peak and then decrease as amorphous disorder develops.
Above 900 K, total dislocation line length decreases significantly because of dislocation annihilation or starvation.
Pure Cu typically undergoes monotonic thermal softening without the complex friction spike attributed to HEA disordering.
The SFE crossover and amorphization-onset temperature may vary by approximately ±50 K because of local composition fluctuations.
A decrease in HCP atom fraction together with a decrease in dislocation line length distinguishes disorder-induced amorphization from mechanical annealing.

contradictions.description: The predicted sequence says HCP atom counts should fall when amorphous disorder develops, but the falsification rule also treats a low HCP fraction during a friction spike as evidence against the disorder/amorphization hypothesis. A single post-indentation low HCP count therefore has contradictory interpretations.

The mechanism attributes decreasing dislocation length to annihilation or starvation associated with disorder, but the same decrease can result from mechanical annealing. The proposed joint decrease in HCP atoms and dislocation length does not by itself distinguish the two mechanisms as claimed.
